Yes... Sort of. People who visit Cuba can now bring back $100 worth of cuban cigars. However, since the embargo has actually not been lifted yet actual importation for sale is still illegal. Because of conditions on the island though, cuban cigars today are not what they once were and they are actually not as sought after as they used to be.

I wouldn't say that Cuban cigars have diminished in quality. One big change is that most of the industry switched to a different type of wrapper called Habano 2000 which is more resistant to blue mold. The wrapper leaf does greatly impact the taste of the cigar, so there was a change. Non-Cuban cigar territories have also adopted Habano 2000 (and other varieties) in order to combat the mold and beetle problems. Cuba has a fairly unique soil profile that imparts the leaves with their distinct taste. And they tend to have the best rollers and quality control in the industry. Still, non-Cuban cigars can be every bit as good (or better) and can be purchased at a fraction of the price. Handmade Cuban cigars are not cheap, regardless if they're legal or not. Most non-Cuban cigars are not "puros" (i.e. cigars produced from tobacco of one nation). That allows them to use (for example) a wrapper leaf from Connecticut, a Mexican binder, and filler from Nicaragua in order to blend a more complex smoke.

When the embargo is lifted, I'd expect prices for Cubans to jump astronomically given the demand in the US. I'm not sure how quickly they'll be able to ramp up production to meet demand--tobacco is cured & aged so it will probably take years for the supply of quality Cuban tobacco to rise in order to meet this demand.
